speakerBio: Has seen too many thunderclap headaches sent home and preaches the CT-then-LP rule.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 45-year-old describes "the worst headache of my life," maximal the instant it began, with a stiff neck and photophobia. The CT six hours later looks normal — and that is exactly the trap. Subarachnoid haemorrhage is diagnosed by taking the thunderclap seriously and not stopping at a negative early scan.

1 · The headache that must never be dismissed

A thunderclap headache — maximal at onset, "like being hit on the head" — is a subarachnoid haemorrhage until definitively excluded, no matter how well the patient looks now.

Most SAH is from a ruptured saccular (berry) aneurysm; other causes include perimesencephalic (benign) bleeds and AVMs. Presentation: sudden severe headache ± transient loss of consciousness, vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia, and sometimes a sentinel "warning" bleed days before.

2 · Diagnosis — CT then LP

  • Non-contrast CT is highly sensitive in the first 6 hours, but sensitivity falls with time as blood disperses.
  • If CT is negative but suspicion persists, do a lumbar puncture at ≥12 hours looking for xanthochromia (bilirubin from breakdown of red cells — distinguishes true SAH from a traumatic tap).
  • Once SAH is confirmed, CT angiography (or catheter angiography) locates the aneurysm for treatment.

3 · Grading

ScaleBased on
Hunt & Hess / WFNSClinical severity (consciousness, deficit) — predicts outcome
Modified FisherAmount of blood on CT — predicts vasospasm risk

4 · Securing the aneurysm — stop the rebleed

💡 Rebleeding is the early killer

An unsecured aneurysm can rebleed catastrophically within hours to days. Secure it early by endovascular coiling or surgical clipping; the ISAT trial favoured coiling for suitable aneurysms (better outcomes), though clipping is chosen by anatomy and multidisciplinary decision. Keep BP controlled and avoid straining until secured.

5 · The delayed complications (the reason for ICU)

ComplicationTimingManagement
RebleedingHours–daysSecure aneurysm early; BP control
Delayed cerebral ischaemia / vasospasmDay 4–14Nimodipine (improves outcome), euvolaemia, treat with induced hypertension ± endovascular therapy
HydrocephalusEarly or lateExternal ventricular drain / shunt
HyponatraemiaDaysCerebral salt wasting vs SIADH — maintain euvolaemia; avoid fluid restriction if salt wasting
Seizures, cardiac stunning (neurogenic)VariableSupportive
☠️ M&M — the negative CT that wasn't the end

A patient with a thunderclap headache had a normal CT at eight hours and was discharged with "migraine"; no LP was done. Five days later the aneurysm rebled and she died. Lesson: a negative CT beyond the first few hours does not exclude SAH — a thunderclap headache needs a CT and, if negative and still suspected, an LP for xanthochromia. Miss the sentinel bleed and you miss the only chance to secure the aneurysm before the fatal one.

6 · Take-home

  • Thunderclap headache = SAH until excluded — CT, then LP at ≥12 h for xanthochromia if CT negative.
  • Secure the aneurysm early (coiling favoured by ISAT) to prevent rebleeding.
  • Nimodipine and euvolaemia for delayed cerebral ischaemia/vasospasm (day 4–14).
  • Watch for hydrocephalus and hyponatraemia.

moderatorQs.q: Why isn't a negative CT enough to exclude SAH?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because CT sensitivity for subarachnoid blood is very high in the first 6 hours but falls with time as blood disperses and haematocrit changes. So a thunderclap headache with a negative CT beyond a few hours still needs a lumbar puncture at ≥12 hours looking for xanthochromia, which distinguishes true SAH from a traumatic tap. Stopping at the negative CT is the classic fatal shortcut.

moderatorQs.q: Coiling or clipping — how do you decide?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Both secure the aneurysm to prevent the early rebleed; the ISAT trial favoured endovascular coiling for suitable aneurysms, with better disability-free survival. The final choice is anatomical and multidisciplinary (neurosurgery + neuroradiology) — some aneurysms are better clipped. The key principle is to secure it early, because an unsecured aneurysm can rebleed catastrophically within hours to days.

moderatorQs.q: What is delayed cerebral ischaemia and how do you manage it?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: It is ischaemia from vasospasm peaking around days 4–14 after SAH, a major cause of late deterioration. Prophylactic nimodipine improves outcome, and you maintain euvolaemia and normal physiology; established DCI is treated with induced hypertension and, if needed, endovascular therapy. The modified Fisher score (blood load on CT) predicts who is at highest risk.

audienceQs.q: The headache resolved and they look well — can I still be worried?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Absolutely — a sentinel (warning) bleed can settle and precede a devastating rupture days later. 'Looks well now' is no reassurance in a thunderclap headache. Image and, if the CT is negative and suspicion persists, do the LP. Catching the sentinel bleed is the whole point.

audienceQs.q: Why is the sodium dropping a few days in?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Hyponatraemia is common after SAH, usually from cerebral salt wasting (renal sodium loss with volume depletion) or SIADH. The distinction matters because the treatment differs — salt wasting needs salt and volume replacement, not fluid restriction. Maintain euvolaemia, because both hypovolaemia and hyponatraemia worsen vasospasm risk.
